Receptors contain a binding site (hollow or cleft on the receptor surface) that is recognized by the chemical messenger (ligand)
Binding of the ligand involves intermolecular bonds and results in an induced fit of the receptor protein
Change in receptor shape can results in a ‘domino’ effect known as signal transduction, leading to a chemical signal being received inside the cell
Chemical messengers (ligands) can bind a receptor on the outside of the cell and departs the receptor (that is to say it is not permanently bound)
Non-covalent interactions are individually regarded as weak and easy to break but collectively quite strong
Optimizing contact distance including surface complementarity allows maximizing of induced dipole – induced dipole attractive forces in hydrophobic regions
In some cases a water molecule can serve as an H-bond bridge between otherwise “out-of-reach” hydrogen bonding interactions
Solvation and desolvation are critical regulators of the binding affinity

If a binding interface is hydrophobic, then release of water from that interface will provide favorable entropy and interaction energy particularly by displacing water molecules in hydrophobic cavities.
Specificity is important to limit non-specific interaction that may otherwise cause false positives for sensors, high background for imaging agents, or side effects for drugs.
Antibodies belong to a class of proteins called immunoglobulins
Antibodies include IgG, IgM, IgA, IgD & IgE
The ability of immunoglobulins to bind antigen is determined by amino acid sequence in the variable region
The antibody molecule has functions of specific binding to antigen eliciting response as well as having biological activity to bind to cells to recruit them to the antigen site.
Sequence variability is not distributed evenly in the variable region of antibodies but is instead localized to the CDR (complementarity determining regions)

Plasmids (or vectors) are circular DNA molecules that are capable of replicating within a host and can be transferred to other cells (note that the replication happens in those cells if the plasmid contains an origin of replication compatible for that host cell) Shuttle vectors are plasmids capable of propagating and transferring (“shuttling”) genes between two different organisms.
Cloning vectors are used to insert foreign DNA and amplify it (make more copies of the DNA for further use)
Expression vectors are used produce mRNA of a gene of interest and must have a region to initiate transcription of RNA (promoter) and must have a region to terminate transcription of RNA (terminator)
RNA synthesis starts at the end of the promoter, which is a highly conserved sequence at the 5’ end of a gene.
RNA elongation occurs until RNA polymerase encounters a termination sequence on the DNA where the RNA polymerase releases the growing single stranded RNA and the DNA template
Prokaryotic and eukaryotic genes have regulatory DNA sequences that interact with proteins that are used to help switch the gene on or off.

The lac operon has 3 genes each involved in processing the sugar lactose where one of them is the gene (lacZ) for the enzyme β-galactosidase and this enzyme hydrolyses lactose to yield glucose and galactose

For the lac operon, little to no β-galactosidase is produced in these three scenarios: 1) When glucose is present and lactose is absent 2) When glucose is present and lactose is present 3) When glucose is absent and lactose is absent However, the lac operon does allow production of β-galactosidase when glucose is absent and lactose is present
Some forms of DNA polymerase can remove mismatched bases by proofreading which eliminates incorrect nucleotides immediately after they are added to the growing DNA during replication.
Chromosome level mutations include: deletions; inversions; translocations; duplications
Taq polymerase is useful because it survives the melting temperature of DNA denaturation
Quantitative PCR uses fluorescently labeled primers to develop time-point data to help discern how much DNA (or RNA) was originally in the sample.

A multiple cloning site is an area of the plasmid vector that contains many common restriction enzyme sites to provide a choice of restriction enzyme sites to use when you cut your DNA of interest and put it in the plasmid.

X-Gal turns blue when its beta glycosidic bond is cleaved by the product of the lacZ; therefore, when the lacZ is intact it makes a blue color when expressed if X-Gal is present and contrastingly if the lacZ gene is disrupted, the bacteria appear white because no lacZ product is formed.

For directional cloning two cuts with two different restriction enzymes are made in the vector and the two same restriction enzymes are used construct a foreign DNA insert allowing the insert to be assembled into the vector in a specific direction. To express a eukaryotic protein in E. coli, the eukaryotic cDNA must be cloned in an expression vector that contains an appropriate, promoter, ribosome binding site, and ideally a transcriptional terminator

Using recombinant DNA technology, collections of billions of peptides or proteins can be presented on phage and these phage-display libraries can be surveyed for specific affinity or activity of the displayed peptide or protein.
Chemical genetics is the use of synthetic or exogenous ligands to alter the function of a single gene product within the context of a single or multicellular environment.

In forward chemical genetics, the goal is target identification where screening large sets of small molecules is used to cause a specific phenotype of interest and ultimately used to isolate and identify the protein target that generates such a phenotype
In reverse chemical genetics, the goal is target function and validation to screen for compounds that bind to a given protein.

Epigenetics are non-genetic factors that cause the organism's genes to express a certain way (increased or decrease expression) and this effect on the genetic expression levels can in some cases last through several generations.
Histones are an octamer protein complex with positive charge residues that if modified by acetylation are believed to lower the charge of the histone thereby loosening the associated DNA.
Nucleosomes are the complex of DNA wrapped around the 2 copies of the 4 different histone protein cores (2x4 so a single histone is an octomer)
Loose chromatin structure called euchromatin allows RNA polymerase to bind and make mRNA
Heterochromatin are chromatin structures where DNA is tightly wrapped around structural proteins causes inactivation of the gene by preventing expression.
Much of the genome is packaged in heterochromatin.
Posttranslational modification of the histone tails help determine the chromatin packaging state.

All of the core histones have an unstructured N-terminal tail of about 30 amino acids which is the site of extensive post-translational modification that changes protein-DNA interaction and serve as signals for docking of other proteins.
DNA methylation can inhibit transcription factor binding and also recruit Methyl CpG Binding Domain proteins which can recruit/modify histones
Methylation allows environmental factors to quickly control gene expression without making permanent mutations
DNA methylation is found in CpG (CG) dinucleotides in humans, with the cytosines on both strand typically being methylated as 5-Methyl Cytosine.

HAT (histone acetyltransferase) are activators of gene expression by adding acetyl groups to histone tails thereby loosening the DNA/histone interaction HDAC (histone deacetylases) are repressors of gene expression by removing acetyl groups thereby restoring the positive charge allowing the tight interaction between histones and the DNA.
Viruses are often considered non-living since they do not independently carry out metabolism, but can still evolve and replicate inside of host cells.
Filamentous bacteriophage known as M13 can reproduce without killing E. coli cell.
In metabolic engineering, the addition of genes can be used to change a target phenotype.
Mutant clones can be identified to have a certain trait by selection and screening processes
